AL-01.name: Probabilistic Reasoning Calibration
AL-01.definition: distinguishing a model's linguistic confidence from factual accuracy, preventing fluency from being mistaken for correctness.

AL-02.name: Algorithmic Mechanism Grasp
AL-02.definition: understanding that AI derives answers via statistical pattern completion, not logical deduction or true world-modeling.

AL-03.name: Context Window Awareness
AL-03.definition: tracking and anticipating memory degradation over extended interactions, enabling proactive re-anchoring of critical context.

AL-04.name: Structural Brittleness Anticipation
AL-04.definition: foreseeing exactly where an AI will break nested data, complex formatting, deep conditionality, or recursive logic.

AL-05.name: Domain-Grounding Aptitude
AL-05.definition: establishing a specific knowledge environment and custom parameters before directing AI on specialized or sensitive tasks.

AL-06.name: Stochastic Output Variance Awareness
AL-06.definition: understanding that identical prompts can produce meaningfully different outputs across invocations, requiring probabilistic rather than deterministic expectations.

AL-07.name: Capability Boundary Mapping
AL-07.definition: active mental cartography of what a model can reliably execute versus where its performance characteristically degrades.

AL-08.name: Training Data Recency Sensitivity
AL-08.definition: awareness of a model's knowledge cutoff and the instinct to flag temporally sensitive claims for independent verification.

AL-09.name: Model-Task Fit Assessment
AL-09.definition: meta-judgment of whether a given model's architecture, training modality, and capability profile is appropriate for the task.

AL-10.name: AI Epistemic State Modeling
AL-10.definition: mentally simulating what information the AI does and does not have in its current context window, predicting its likely failure modes before output.

AL-11.name: Multi-modal Situational Literacy
AL-11.definition: understanding that AI processes images, code, audio, structured data, and text with different reliability profiles, adjusting verification depth per modality.

AL-12.name: System Constraint Awareness
AL-12.definition: recognizing the invisible instruction layers (system prompts, safety filters, alignment) that bound behavior, distinguishing constraint-imposed refusal from genuine capability failure.

AL-13.name: Prompt Injection Vulnerability Awareness
AL-13.definition: security awareness that externally sourced content can carry malicious instructions that hijack AI behavior, prompting sandboxing and source verification.

PR-01.name: Negative Constraint Application
PR-01.definition: explicitly defining exclusion parameters (what the AI must not produce/assume/include) to eliminate unwanted output space.

PR-02.name: Cognitive Scaffolding
PR-02.definition: structuring a directive to force sequential, multi-step reasoning rather than a single-shot probabilistic guess.

PR-03.name: Contextual Density Optimization
PR-03.definition: calibrating the ratio of background context to core directive to maximize signal-to-noise without overwhelming generative focus.

PR-04.name: Strategic Query Pivoting
PR-04.definition: abandoning a failed linguistic framing and reconstructing the query from a structurally different angle rather than repeating it.

PR-05.name: Output Topology Definition
PR-05.definition: mentally visualizing and explicitly commanding the structural architecture of the output before generation.

PR-06.name: Persona Anchoring
PR-06.definition: defining a specific expert role/epistemic posture for the AI to inhabit, modulating the character of its reasoning.

PR-07.name: Inductive Example Provisioning
PR-07.definition: supplying few-shot pattern templates that establish desired behavior by concrete demonstration rather than abstract instruction.

PR-08.name: Decomposition Precision
PR-08.definition: atomizing complex goals into minimal, non-overlapping sub-tasks so each AI invocation has a single unambiguous objective.

PR-09.name: Constraint Hierarchy Definition
PR-09.definition: explicitly ranking constraint priority so the AI resolves conflicts predictably under competing directives.

PR-10.name: Ambiguity Pre-emption
PR-10.definition: identifying semantic misinterpretation points before submission and resolving lexical/referential ambiguity proactively.

PR-11.name: Verification Checkpoint Embedding
PR-11.definition: building explicit self-audit instructions into the directive, directing the AI to test its output against criteria before concluding.

PR-12.name: Iterative Refinement Patience
PR-12.definition: treating prompt construction as progressive multi-cycle optimization, tolerating refinement loops without premature closure.

PR-13.name: Semantic Precision Sensitivity
PR-13.definition: awareness that minor lexical choices (synonyms, tense, quantifiers, presuppositions) produce divergent outputs, driving word-level optimization beyond mere clarity.

PR-14.name: Recursive Self-Critique Elicitation
PR-14.definition: directing the AI to adversarially evaluate its own prior output, engineering an endogenous quality-control loop before human review.

PR-15.name: Parallel Task Architecture
PR-15.definition: identifying which decomposed sub-tasks are logically independent and can be dispatched simultaneously, exploiting parallelism for throughput.

EC-01.name: Factual Hallucination Detection
EC-01.definition: identifying fabricated, confabulated, or misattributed information presented with the surface texture of established fact.

EC-02.name: Syntactical and Structural Debugging
EC-02.definition: identifying logic gaps, missing steps, broken dependencies, or code misalignments in procedural/technical output.

EC-03.name: Internal Contradiction Recognition
EC-03.definition: catching conflicting logic, changing premises, or self-negating arguments within a single response.

EC-04.name: Algorithmic Traceability
EC-04.definition: stepping backward through AI logic to identify the precise origin of an error within a single output.

EC-05.name: Physical and Spatial Logic Verification
EC-05.definition: validating AI descriptions of physical laws, spatial relationships, and systems logic against real-world constraints.

EC-06.name: Isolated Verification Rigor
EC-06.definition: testing AI-generated claims/code/logic in a conceptually isolated sandbox before integrating into live production.

EC-07.name: Omission Detection
EC-07.definition: identifying content silently left out of the AI's reasoning within a single response (missing qualifications, absent steps). Scope distinct from EC-13 and EC-14.

EC-08.name: Statistical Plausibility Assessment
EC-08.definition: order-of-magnitude sanity-checking of numerical claims, statistics, and quantitative outputs before acceptance.

EC-09.name: Temporal Coherence Validation
EC-09.definition: verifying that AI sequences, timelines, and causal chains maintain consistent temporal ordering and directional causality.

EC-10.name: Scope Boundary Enforcement
EC-10.definition: detecting when output has silently expanded beyond defined task parameters, adding unrequested, unreviewed scope.

EC-11.name: Confidence-Accuracy Decoupling
EC-11.definition: resisting the treatment of assertive, fluent output as implicitly more accurate; uniform scrutiny regardless of surface confidence.

EC-12.name: Error Propagation Tracing
EC-12.definition: recognizing that an early seeded error has cascaded through locally-consistent but systemically-compromised downstream outputs.

EC-13.name: Edge Case Coverage Audit
EC-13.definition: systematically enumerating boundary conditions and minority scenarios that statistically-anchored defaults silently excluded.

EC-14.name: Hidden Assumption Excavation
EC-14.definition: surfacing and challenging the invisible load-bearing premises an AI's reasoning depends on but never states.

ES-01.name: Privacy and Anonymization Foresight
ES-01.definition: filtering and stripping PII and confidential information before it enters an AI interaction.

ES-02.name: Demographic and Cultural Bias Detection
ES-02.definition: identifying skewed assumptions, statistical stereotyping, or cultural blindness in AI reasoning/content.

ES-03.name: Regulatory Compliance Adherence
ES-03.definition: evaluating outputs against external legal, safety, professional, or enterprise governance frameworks.

ES-04.name: Epistemic Vigilance
ES-04.definition: refusing AI as a primary authority; reflexively cross-referencing claims against primary sources.

ES-05.name: Intellectual Property Sensitivity
ES-05.definition: recognizing when output reproduces, paraphrases, or structurally derives copyrighted/proprietary work without transformation.

ES-06.name: Dual-Use Risk Assessment
ES-06.definition: evaluating whether a legitimate output could be weaponized or cause harm in a different context or by a different actor.

ES-07.name: Psychological Manipulation Detection
ES-07.definition: identifying when persuasive output crosses from legitimate influence into manipulation exploiting cognitive/emotional vulnerabilities.

ES-08.name: AI Disclosure Judgment
ES-08.definition: knowing when transparency about AI's role is legally required, organizationally mandated, or morally necessary, and acting unprompted.

ES-09.name: Value-Outcome Alignment Verification
ES-09.definition: confirming recommendations are congruent with actual human/organizational values and long-term goals, not merely constraint-compliant.

ES-10.name: Autonomy-Preservation Vigilance
ES-10.definition: awareness that habitual deference erodes independent decision-making, with the counter-reflex to exercise judgment on consequential decisions.

ES-11.name: Accountability Attribution Clarity
ES-11.definition: explicitly assigning professional/legal/moral responsibility for an AI-assisted output to a specific human before deployment.

ES-12.name: Systemic Scale Impact Reasoning
ES-12.definition: reasoning beyond single-use to second- and third-order societal consequences of the same output pattern deployed at population scale.

ES-13.name: Data Provenance Interrogation
ES-13.definition: examining the likely composition and embedded biases of the training data behind an output, especially in minority/non-Western domains.

ES-14.name: Consent and Agency Stewardship
ES-14.definition: verifying that outputs representing or affecting other humans preserve their consent, autonomy, dignity, and material interests, including in automated contexts.

CS-01.name: Semantic Blending
CS-01.definition: smoothing transitions between human- and AI-authored blocks, eliminating tonal discontinuity in the final artifact.

CS-02.name: Dependency Preservation
CS-02.definition: integrating output without breaking existing logical dependencies, narrative threads, data pipelines, or hierarchies.

CS-03.name: Information Density Pruning
CS-03.definition: stripping verbose, repetitive AI filler to extract only high-signal insight.

CS-04.name: Authorial Tone Alignment
CS-04.definition: editing AI vocabulary, syntax, and cadence to match a pre-established human or organizational voice.

CS-05.name: Cross-Domain Translation
CS-05.definition: restructuring technical output for a non-specialist audience without loss of accuracy.

CS-06.name: Inferential Gap Bridging
CS-06.definition: completing logical/contextual gaps the AI left implicit but which a human reader requires made explicit.

CS-07.name: Salience Hierarchy Reconstruction
CS-07.definition: re-ranking information by actual domain relevance rather than the AI's default statistical co-occurrence ordering.

CS-08.name: Multi-Source Coherence Integration
CS-08.definition: maintaining consistency when synthesizing outputs across multiple AI calls, sessions, or modalities.

CS-09.name: Attribution Tracking
CS-09.definition: bookkeeping which contributions originated from human reasoning versus AI generation within a synthesized artifact.

CS-10.name: Register Modulation
CS-10.definition: calibrating formality, technicality, and assumed shared knowledge for the specific deployment audience and relationship.

CS-11.name: Uncertainty Transparency Calibration
CS-11.definition: restoring appropriate epistemic hedges to AI claims, counteracting AI's over-assertive stripping of probabilistic hedging.

CD-01.name: Statistical Homogenization Resistance
CD-01.definition: rejecting the AI's most statistically probable/averaged/safe response in favor of the genuinely interesting.

CD-02.name: Lateral Concept Injection
CD-02.definition: introducing metaphors, cultural frames, and references outside the AI's training distribution, forcing genuine novelty.

CD-03.name: Counter-Factual Probing
CD-03.definition: using hypothetical inversions and 'what if' scenarios to stress-test and expand the AI's initial hypothesis.

CD-04.name: Stylistic Idiosyncrasy Retention
CD-04.definition: defending unique formatting, pacing, humor, and edge-case perspectives against the AI's normalizing tendency.

CD-05.name: Aesthetic Discernment
CD-05.definition: evaluating creative output against an internalized human standard of taste, resonance, and intended emotional impact.

CD-06.name: Constraint-Transcendence Instinct
CD-06.definition: recognizing when deliberately violating a stated constraint yields a qualitatively superior outcome than strict compliance.

CD-07.name: Narrative Tension Injection
CD-07.definition: introducing productive conflict, stakes, or irresolution that AI tends to prematurely smooth into consensus.

CD-08.name: Analogical Novelty Generation
CD-08.definition: producing novel analogical mappings and cross-domain metaphors outside AI's statistical co-occurrence patterns.

CD-09.name: Surprise Preservation
CD-09.definition: protecting counterintuitive or unconventional elements from the AI's normalizing tendency.

CD-10.name: Embodied Experience Injection
CD-10.definition: infusing work with sensory, physical, kinesthetic experience unavailable to AI, producing a quality of felt truth.

CD-11.name: Audience Empathy Modeling
CD-11.definition: maintaining a rich, specific model of the audience's emotional state, prior knowledge, and unstated needs (a ToM signature).

AUI-01.name: Cognitive Friction Recognition
AUI-01.definition: identifying the moment a task's demand exceeds optimal manual effort, triggering delegation.

AUI-02.name: Task-Type Delegation Judgment
AUI-02.definition: routing rote/high-volume work to AI while reserving high-nuance, high-stakes, or ethically consequential work for human cognition.

AUI-03.name: Modality Appropriateness
AUI-03.definition: matching the correct type of AI system (generative, analytical, retrieval) to the structural requirements of the problem.

AUI-04.name: Interaction ROI Intuition
AUI-04.definition: recognizing the tipping point where direct human effort beats the compounding cost of debugging a failing prompt chain.

AUI-05.name: Working Memory Offloading
AUI-05.definition: using AI as an external scratchpad to externalize intermediate states, freeing executive function for higher-order reasoning.

AUI-06.name: Cognitive Load Self-Monitoring
AUI-06.definition: real-time awareness of one's own saturation, enabling strategic offloading at the moment of productive overload before degradation.

AUI-07.name: Prompt Investment Calibration
AUI-07.definition: judging how much effort to invest in prompt crafting versus the expected return in output quality.

AUI-08.name: Dependency Risk Awareness
AUI-08.definition: recognizing that sustained delegation creates progressive skill atrophy and cognitive fragility in one's own profile.

AUI-09.name: Handoff Timing Precision
AUI-09.definition: judging exactly when to reclaim agentic control mid-task before autonomous completion introduces irreversible errors or goal drift.

AUI-10.name: Skill-Gap Self-Awareness
AUI-10.definition: inventorying one's own knowledge gaps so AI supplements genuine expertise rather than silently substituting for absent understanding.

AUI-11.name: Verification Effort Calibration
AUI-11.definition: allocating deep review to high-stakes output and lighter review to routine output, optimizing the total verification budget.

AUI-12.name: Agentic Permission Scoping
AUI-12.definition: defining minimum necessary authority, resource access, and reversibility constraints before delegating to autonomous agents.

CA-01.name: Sovereign Override Capacity
CA-01.definition: the willingness to reject AI authority, overrule outputs, and rewrite its core assumptions when they conflict with human judgment.

CA-02.name: Cognitive Momentum Maintenance
CA-02.definition: sustaining parallel productive human thinking rather than going cognitively idle during AI generation waits.

CA-03.name: Contextual Compartmentalization
CA-03.definition: isolating different problems into separate cognitive frames, preventing context cross-contamination across unrelated tasks.

CA-04.name: Interactional Resilience
CA-04.definition: rapidly diagnosing, restructuring, and recovering a workflow when AI has hallucinated or lost context.

CA-05.name: Terminal Feedback Provisioning
CA-05.definition: closing the loop by feeding errors, corrections, and observations back into the session to progressively align AI performance.

CA-06.name: Adaptive Trust Calibration
CA-06.definition: evidence-based adjustment of deference based on real-time performance, preventing both chronic over-trust and paralyzing under-trust.

CA-07.name: Goal Integrity Maintenance
CA-07.definition: maintaining fidelity to original intent across multi-turn interactions, resisting AI-induced goal drift.

CA-08.name: Metacognitive Self-Monitoring
CA-08.definition: continuous awareness of one's own cognitive state, biases, and judgment quality during deep collaboration.

CA-09.name: Process Auditability Discipline
CA-09.definition: maintaining a workflow record sufficient for retrospective audit, attribution, and legal defensibility.

CA-10.name: Selective Attention Governance
CA-10.definition: resisting AI scope expansions and tangential elaborations, anchoring deliberately on the core objective.

CA-11.name: Affective Regulation Under Failure
CA-11.definition: preventing frustration or impatience from degrading decision quality when AI repeatedly fails or hallucinates.

CA-12.name: Cross-Session Transfer Learning
CA-12.definition: extracting generalizable heuristics and failure patterns from past interactions and applying them to novel future tasks.

CA-13.name: Identity Authorship Preservation
CA-13.definition: maintaining a continuous, defensible sense of one's intellectual contribution and creative voice through deep collaboration.

CA-14.name: Intra-Session Pattern Recognition
CA-14.definition: detecting recurring failure patterns and biases in the AI's current-session responses, enabling proactive strategy adjustment.

CA-15.name: AI Sycophancy Resistance
CA-15.definition: recognizing that AI is trained to affirm the user (making agreement unreliable as confirmation) and soliciting adversarial challenge anyway.

CA-16.name: Pre-Generation Epistemic Independence
CA-16.definition: forming one's own hypothesis before reading AI output, preserving an independent baseline against anchoring.

CA-17.name: Vigilance Sustainment
CA-17.definition: maintaining rigorous scrutiny across long sessions, counteracting the temporal decay of evaluation quality from habituation, fatigue, and complacency.
